newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu visits Gabon, battle on road to Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu visits Gabon, battle on road to Kinshasa.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko left Zaire on Wednesday for a mini peace summit in Gabon as reports emerged of a heavy civilian death toll in a battle on the road to his capital Kinshasa.

Residents and other sources said about 200 civilians and more than 100 soldiers from both sides of Zaire's civil war had been killed in fighting around the town of Kenge, 250 km (150 miles) east of Kinshasa.
"There were around 200 civilians killed at Kenge on Tuesday alone. We do not know yet how they were killed," one humanitarian source told Reuters.
Witnesses said Mobutu, who is battling cancer and Kabila's rebels, arrived in Gabon's capital Libreville looking tired and went straight to a waiting vehicle.
He left Kinshasa with many people openly speculating -- or expressing the wish -- that he had gone for good.
"The leopard is finished. He is not coming back," shouted an onlooker outside the aiport as Mobutu's plane took off.
Mobutu, who regularly sports a leopard-skin hat, has dominated Africa's third largest country for three decades.
Aides insisted he would return. "He will be back in 24 or 48 hours," presidential spokesman Kabuya Lumuna said.

The Zaire government said he would discuss the war with the presidents of Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon. Gabon's government newspaper L'Union said the mini-summit would be on Thursday.

On the humanitarian front, the number of Rwandan Hutu refugees flown home from rebel-held Zaire passed the 10,000 mark but relief officials said tens of thousands of others were either dead or missing in the forests.
"We now think we will probably only move around 40,000 refugees back to Rwanda by air," said Peter Kessler of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR. "The rest are either missing or dead."

In Cape Town President Nelson Mandela, who hosted talks between Kabila and Mobutu on a South African ship in the Congolese port of Pointe Noire on Sunday, said he was satisfied Kabila was honouring a pledge to halt his army's march on Kinshasa.
But Kabila told Radio France International that taking the capital was "on the agenda" for the rebels. "Troops are obliged to advance," he said.
Kabila and his commanders, who took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for minority Tutsis, have said they are building up for a final push against the capital.
But reliable reports from the battlefront were scarce and conflicting propaganda claims proliferated.
Independent sources say the army counter-attacked near Kenge on the road to Kinshasa. Rebel radio said on Tuesday it had driven back the counter-attack in a "brief but heavy encounter".
Diplomatic sources say the front line is close to the strategic Kwango River bridge 200 km (125 miles) from Kinshasa.

Western diplomats in Angola's capital Luanda said the Angolan army was increasing its military presence in the oil-rich Cabinda enclave bordering Zaire but the reason for the buildup was not clear. Zaire accuses Angola of backing the rebels.

Air France diverted its scheduled flight from Kinshasa to Congo, on the opposite side of the Zaire river. An airline official said the plane normally stayed nine hours on the ground in Kinshasa, too long under current circumstances.

U.N. officials in Nairobi, quoting rebel radio, said that Kabila's rebels had offered to set up a broad-based national government open to opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi and others but excluding what it called "all Mobutists".
